item.title: ₹5,501 crore worth of ₹2,000 notes are still out there somewhere. And every one of them is still legal…
item.dc:creator: Fin shots · Instagram
item.description:
₹5,501 crore worth of ₹2,000 notes are still out there somewhere. And every one of them is still legal tender!

The note came in November 2016, right after demonetisation, to put cash back into the system quickly. By March 2018, ₹6.73 lakh crore worth were in circulation. The RBI stopped printing them in 2018-19 and announced their withdrawal in May 2023. Over 98% have since come back.

If you find one in an old wallet or cupboard, you can still deposit it at any of the RBI’s 19 Issue Offices or send it through India Post.

Do you still have a ₹2,000 note lying around somewhere? Let us know in the comments and follow @finshots.in for more such content!

item.title: Tarluvada, a village near Vizag, was once known for its marigolds and jasmine. Now it’s home to Google’s…
item.dc:creator: Fin shots · Instagram
item.description:
Tarluvada, a village near Vizag, was once known for its marigolds and jasmine. Now it’s home to Google’s $15 billion AI hub.

India’s data centre boom is usually sold as the country catching up. But global tech giants lease about 60% of the capacity, while facilities used by Indian entities account for less than 13%. Meanwhile, India supplies the land, the water, round-the-clock coal power and a tax holiday till 2047.

An economic idea from the 1970s called World Systems Theory explains why this pattern keeps repeating. Swipe through to see how it plays out in India’s data centres.

Should India keep offering tax breaks to data centres that mostly serve customers abroad?

Let us know in the comments and follow
@finshots.in for more such content!

item.title: Is pollution shrinking India’s economy?...
item.dc:creator: Fin shots · Instagram
item.description:
Is pollution shrinking India’s economy?

India ranked 176th out of 177 countries in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index. But the price tag is steeper than the rank. Pollution costs Indian businesses $260 billion in lost revenue in 2024, about 6% of GDP.

That bill has nearly tripled in three years. Do you think India is treating pollution like the economic problem it has become? Tell us in the comments!
